jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: Internal Candidate
jokes.joke: I applied to be a corrections officer. They asked if I was adaptable. I said, “Absolutely—I can change.” The warden slid my résumé back and said, “That’s what everyone in here says.” I didn’t get the job, but they did move up my parole hearing.

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Career Day
jokes.joke: I'm a workaholic, so I became a corrections officer, because I wanted a job where the people I'm mad at literally cannot leave the building either. My wife says I bring work home with me. No I don't. I bring home the belief that everyone's lying about where they were last night, and that's different.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Cell Checks
jokes.joke: I just found out I’m dealing with an unexpected pregnancy. It’s a pretty massive lifestyle shift. You go from having your own hobbies and free time to suddenly becoming a corrections officer for a tiny, suicidal drunk person. My entire future now is just doing 3 AM cell checks to make sure my inmate hasn't managed to choke on a rogue Lego.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Project Baby
jokes.joke: I'm a workaholic, so when my wife announced an unexpected pregnancy, I didn't freak out—I opened Excel. Nine-month timeline, critical path for the delivery, risk matrix for sleepless nights, and a Gantt chart tracking every kick. At the end I asked, "Does this project come with stock options, or just unlimited unpaid overtime?"

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Country Road Confession
jokes.joke: I was driving down this empty country road when my GPS suddenly said, “In two miles, prepare for an unexpected development.” I panicked—last time I heard something like that, my cousin announced a surprise pregnancy at Thanksgiving. I pulled over like, “Look, if this road is about to give me a baby, I am not emotionally equipped for that level of roadside assistance.”

scores.comment: Clear premise and solid second turn; the suspicious-spouse payoff is amusing but not especially sharp.
Strong, accessible baby-as-inmate comparison with vivid escalation; slightly familiar framing, but it lands.
Competently structured, but the Excel-project-manager angle and unpaid-overtime punchline are highly predictable.
The road-giving-birth premise is novel but strained, and the final roadside-assistance line produces more whimsy than laughter.
Clean double-meaning on 'adaptable/change,' escalates to a genuine reveal-twist ending that recontextualizes the whole bit.
Strong sustained metaphor (baby as inmate) with a vivid, specific closing image; solid but the payoff is more clever than a big laugh.
Familiar 'workaholic maps everything to spreadsheets' shape; competent execution but predictable turn and closing line.
Fun GPS pun opener but the bit drifts and the closing line is muddled rather than a clean punch.
Solid misdirection that successfully recontextualizes the narrator as an inmate. The punchline is clean, though slightly telegraphed by the word 'change'.
Strong natural stand-up rhythm. The first half is a decent setup, but the turn at the end about interrogating family members elevates it into a highly believable human joke.
Relies on the overused AI trope of applying spreadsheet and corporate project management jargon to domestic life. Competent but generic.
The logic bridging a GPS direction to roadside obstetrics is strained. The absurdity feels forced rather than arriving at a natural comic realization.
Clean prison-application turn with solid parole payoff.
Serviceable premise; suspicion punchline lands mildly.
Strong inmate-baby image and Lego closer carry it.
GPS-pregnancy link feels strained and under-delivered.
Clean premise with a neat final turn; mildly funny and well‑paced.
Solid first‑person angle with a clear comic voice; good closing contrast.
Strong metaphor with vivid imagery; the Lego line lands well.
Competent and clear, but the turn is familiar and the closer is mild.
